newsitem.title: USA: Direction, timing of next Fed move unclear-experts.
newsitem.headline: Direction, timing of next Fed move unclear-experts.

text.p: The Federal Reserve concluded its last meeting of 1996 by leaving interest rates unchanged and the door wide open to speculation about the direction and timing of its next move, Fed watchers said on Tuesday.

"As the Fed looks forward into the first half of 1997, there is no sign of imbalance that could throw the economy off the intended path," said Nomura Securities International Inc chief economist David Resler. "Until it becomes clear the economy is veering off course, it's impossible to predict the direction or the timing of the next Fed move," he added.
The Fed, which last set the federal funds rate at 5.25 percent and the discount rate at 5.0 percent on February 1, has seen the longest stretch of policy inaction since 1993.
"It's fairly rare for the Fed to go on for so long with policy unchanged. It shows the economy is performing as intended by the Fed," Resler, a former Fed economist, added.

"It should be clear by now the unemployment rate is not a guiding force of monetary policy," Resler added. "If it were, and with the unemployment rate below 6.0 percent for more than two years, they would have long tightened and continued to tighten."
Wall Street analysts had expected the Fed's inaction despite Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's recent expression of concern about possible overvaluation of financial assets.
The Dow industrials surged 50 points following the Fed's announcement that reassured market players about the steady cost of financing investments.
"The stock market is not an object of policy. We have more a sense of two-way price action, at least for the time being," Resler noted, in reference to the Dow's recent correction.
Wrightson and Associates chief economist Lou Crandall did not expect a move until broad-based inflation signs emerge.

"Wage pressures will remain a constant theme in the first half of 1997," Crandall said, "but the Fed is unlikely to tighten unless there is corresponding pressure on industrial prices which are currently so soft." Crandall did not expect such price hikes to occur in early 1997.
Crandall said the Fed is now dealing with the opposite situation to that in 1994, when it preemptively tightened in the face of stagnant wages and soaring industrial prices.
"The Fed won't tolerate the same pressure on the crude and intermediate producer price index as they did then, because we have the wage pressures you didn't have then," Crandall said.
But Crandall said, "The most likely direction of the next Fed move is still a tightening."
Chase Securities Inc senior economist James Glassman said, "The Fed is still closer to tightening than they are to easing," although the timing of the move is unclear.
"When that (tightening) happens would be decided by the underlying inflation trend," Glassman added.
However, Glassman, a former Fed Board economist, cautioned against regarding Fed policy as no longer preemptive.

"People think they (Fed officials) are going to be reactive," Glassman said, "but the Fed cares a lot about market psychology and market expectations." Glassman expects the Fed to move before a series of economic numbers show an overheating economy or higher inflation.
"It won't allow itself to fall behind the market's psychology," he said.
Fed officials have told Reuters the central bank had been concerned in 1994 about the Treasury market's overreaction to its string of incremental tightening moves.
"It's obvious from the FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) minutes they (FOMC members) are very nervous about how markets would react when they change direction of policy," Glassman added.
